title: Noise on Real Devices
summary: T1 relaxation, T2 dephasing, readout and gate errors, and how an idle qubit loses population and coherence.
objectives: Turn T1, T2 and a waiting time into the strength of the two noise channels
Predict how much population and coherence a waiting qubit has left
Say why T2 can never be more than twice T1
mission: An idle qubit is the simplest noise experiment on a device. Start a qubit in |+⟩ and let it wait t_wait with relaxation time T1 and coherence time T2. In the QNode idle(T1, T2, t_wait), apply amplitude damping followed by phase damping so that the population of |1⟩ decays as exp(−t/T1) and the coherence as exp(−t/T2). Then store in p1 the probability of measuring 1 and in coherence the size |ρ01| of the off-diagonal element.

prediction.question: A qubit has T1 = 50 µs and a measured T2 = 80 µs. What is its pure dephasing time Tφ?
options: 30 µs, the difference between T2 and T1
prediction.explanation: Relaxation already contributes a coherence rate 1/(2·T1) = 1/100 µs⁻¹. The measured rate is 1/T2 = 1/80 µs⁻¹, so the pure dephasing supplies the rest: 1/80 − 1/100 = 1/400. Tφ is therefore 400 µs, much longer than T2, because relaxation does most of the damage. The rates add; the times do not.

hints: How does amplitude damping with parameter γ change ρ11? Choose γ so that the population falls as exp(−t_wait/T1), and apply qml.AmplitudeDamping(gamma, wires=0).

Amplitude damping also shrinks the coherence, by exp(−t/(2·T1)). The target is exp(−t/T2), so the missing decay comes from pure dephasing: 1/Tφ = 1/T2 − 1/(2·T1). Phase damping multiplies the coherence by √(1 − λ), and you need that to equal exp(−t/Tφ).

Put both channels after the Hadamard gate: amplitude damping, then phase damping with λ = 1 − exp(−2·t_wait/Tφ). Outside the QNode, rho = idle(T1, T2, t_wait) is the density matrix; read ρ11 and ρ01 from its entries.

challenge.mission: The mission turned T1 and T2 into a circuit. In the lab the problem runs the other way: you measure the decay and have to find the times. The variables delays (in µs), p1_data and coh_data hold the population of |1⟩ and the size of the coherence |ρ01| of an idle qubit prepared in |+⟩, measured after each delay with a little noise, so both curves start at 1/2. Store in T1_fit and T2_fit your estimates in µs, and in Tphi_fit the pure dephasing time that follows from them. The validator accepts T1_fit and T2_fit within 10% of the true times and Tphi_fit within 20%, and it requires your three numbers to obey 1/T2 = 1/(2·T1) + 1/Tφ.
hints: What does the logarithm of an exponential decay look like when you plot it against the delay? Which feature of that picture gives the decay time?

np.polyfit(delays, np.log(p1_data), 1) returns the slope and the intercept of a straight line. The slope is minus the decay rate, and the intercept takes care of the factor 1/2 without any extra work.
Do the same with coh_data to get the rate 1/T2. For the pure dephasing, subtract rates and not times: the coherence rate is 1/(2·T1) plus 1/Tφ.

messages.ch_far_t1: T1_fit is {actual} µs, too far from what the population data allow. Fit the logarithm of p1_data against delays, and remember that the slope is −1/T1.
messages.ch_far_t2: T1 is fine, but T2_fit is {actual} µs, too far from what the coherence data allow. Use coh_data for T2, not p1_data, and take the reciprocal of minus the slope.
messages.ch_inconsistent: Tphi_fit is {tphi} µs, but your T1_fit and T2_fit imply {implied} µs. Rates add, so 1/Tφ = 1/T2 − 1/(2·T1); subtracting the times gives something else.
messages.ch_far_tphi: Tphi_fit is {actual} µs. It follows your T1 and T2, but both fits are noisy and the difference of rates amplifies the error, so it is too far from the true value. Fit all the points, not only two of them.
